producers.note: DfE has published no costing of extending free hours to every child from 9 months. Asked the annual cost of extending the 30 hours to non-working parents (written answer 17308, 4 August 2026), it gave none; the answer says 'Nearly 1.5 million children aged 9 months to school age are excluded from the full 30-hour entitlement'. Its 2023 expansion costing note (about £4.1bn by 2027-28) scores the baseline. Written answer 28019 (14 September 2026) values the 30 hours the £100,000 limit withholds at £446m to £874m in 2025/26, at full take-up and full use: a different quantity from the analysis's 15 hours for all.
The SFC's list applies to Scotland-scoped analyses; this one is UK-wide.

producers.note: Reforming childcare subsidies (Gillian Paull, CASE, with the Early Education and Childcare Coalition, 19 October 2026) models replacing Tax-Free Childcare and UC childcare support with one subsidy for working families that tapers with earnings. The LSE release gives its cost only as a percentage of an unstated base ('the increase in subsidy costs for the Government is estimated to be 15% for an hourly subsidy compared to 56% for the smooth subsidy rate'), on Family Resources Survey data updated to 2026/27, assuming parents do not change their work patterns or childcare use. The report at https://www.earlyeducationchildcare.org/reforming-childcare-subsidies refused every fetch (403), so there is no primary to stage (harvest rule 8). Its options cover working families, taper the rate with earnings and absorb the UC element, unlike the analysis's flat 75% subsidy for all.
